title: Cloud Types
keyIdea: Air always holds some water vapour, a gas you cannot see. When damp air rises, it cools, and the vapour condenses into tiny drops of water (or bits of ice, if it is cold enough). Millions of these drops make a cloud. There are three main kinds: cumulus are fluffy heaps with flat bottoms, stratus are flat grey layers, and cirrus are thin wisps high up, made of ice. The kind of cloud is a clue to the weather: small cumulus mean fair weather, stratus often bring a dull day or drizzle, and cumulus that grow tall and dark bring showers.
familyTip: Look out of the window together each morning for a week. Draw the clouds and name them: heap (cumulus), layer (stratus) or wisp (cirrus). Write down what the weather did later that day. On a cold day, breathe on a window or a cold spoon: the mist you see is your breath's water vapour condensing into tiny drops, just like a cloud.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: lift damp air until a cloud forms, zoom in to join drops into rain, sort high and low clouds, name skies and read them as a forecast.

kid: Air has water vapour in it. It is a gas, so you can not see it. When warm, damp air rises, it gets colder. The cold turns the vapour into tiny drops of water. This is called condensation. Millions of tiny drops make a cloud.
The drops in a cloud are so small and light that they float. When lots of them bump and join, a drop gets big and heavy. Then it falls as rain.

There are three main kinds of cloud. Cumulus means heap: fluffy heaps with flat bottoms. Stratus means layer: a flat grey sheet. Cirrus means curl of hair: thin wisps very high up. Up there it is so cold that cirrus are made of bits of ice.
Clouds are clues to the weather. Small white cumulus mean a dry day. Grey stratus can bring drizzle. When cumulus grow tall and dark, a heavy shower is coming.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. Clouds link to Year 4 science in England (evaporation and condensation in the water cycle, and how temperature changes state) and to NGSS K-ESS2-1 and 3-ESS2-1 on weather patterns. The Met Office groups clouds into ten main types; the three basic forms are cumulus (heaped), stratus (layered) and cirrus (wispy, high, ice crystals). Key words: water vapour, condense, condensation, droplet, ice crystal, cumulus, stratus, cirrus.

Common mistakes: thinking clouds are made of steam, smoke or water vapour (vapour is invisible; a cloud is liquid drops or ice); thinking clouds form when air warms up; thinking every cloud brings rain; thinking dark clouds are dirty. A storm cloud looks dark because it is thick enough to block sunlight.

Air cools as it rises because the pressure falls and it expands. The height where cloud forms is where the air has cooled to its dew point. You do not need these terms yet, but they explain why cloud bases often look flat.

In the lab your child lifts a bubble of damp air until it reaches the cold-enough line and a cloud appears, zooms in to join droplets into a raindrop, sorts high icy clouds from low watery ones, names drawn skies, and matches each sky to the weather it brings.

practice.prompt: What is a cloud made of?
choices: Tiny drops of water or bits of ice
practice.hint: Think about what happens to water vapour when air cools down.
practice.explain: A cloud is millions of tiny drops of water, or bits of ice when it is very cold. Steam is hot; clouds are cold.

practice.prompt: On the ground it is {a}°C. A bubble of air rises and cools by {b}°C. What temperature is it now?
practice.hint: The air cools, so the temperature goes down. Take away.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}°C. Rising air cools, which is how clouds form.

practice.prompt: A flat grey sheet of cloud covers the whole sky. Which kind is it?
practice.hint: Stratus means layer. Which cloud is a flat layer?
practice.explain: Stratus is a flat grey layer. It often gives a dull day, sometimes with drizzle.

practice.prompt: Kai drew the clouds for a week. He saw cumulus on {a} days and stratus on {b} days. How many days did he see these two kinds?
practice.hint: Add the cumulus days and the stratus days.

practice.prompt: Why are cirrus clouds made of ice?
choices: They are so high that it is below freezing
They are near the cold sea
Ice is lighter than water vapour
practice.hint: The higher you go, the colder the air gets.
practice.explain: Cirrus are very high up, where the air is far below freezing, so the water turns into tiny bits of ice.

pool.hint: Cold makes water vapour turn back into drops. Where is the air colder?
pool.explain: As damp air rises it cools. The water vapour condenses into tiny drops, and a cloud forms.

pool.prompt: Which cloud is a fluffy heap with a flat bottom?
pool.hint: Cumulus means heap. Which cloud looks like a heap?
pool.explain: Cumulus clouds are fluffy heaps with flat bottoms. Small ones mean fair weather.

pool.prompt: Why do cloud drops not fall as rain straight away?
choices: They are too small and light
Clouds are bags that hold them
The wind holds them up for ever
pool.hint: Think about the size of each drop in a cloud.
pool.explain: Cloud drops are tiny and light, so they float. Only when many join into a big, heavy drop does it fall.

pool.prompt: Cumulus clouds are growing tall and dark in the afternoon. What weather is likely?
pool.hint: Tall, thick heaps hold lots of big drops.
pool.explain: When cumulus grow tall and dark, they hold lots of big drops. Heavy showers, and maybe thunder, are likely.

pool.prompt: You breathe on a cold window and it goes misty. What happened?
choices: Water vapour in your breath condensed
pool.hint: The window is cold. What does cold do to water vapour?
pool.explain: The cold glass cooled the water vapour in your breath, and it condensed into tiny drops, just like a cloud.

pool.prompt: A cloud base is {a} hundred metres up. A cirrus cloud is {b} hundred metres higher. How many hundred metres up is the cirrus?
pool.hint: The cirrus is higher, so add the extra height.
pool.explain: {a} add {b} is {=a+b} hundred metres. Cirrus are much higher than low clouds.

pool.prompt: In {a} days, {b} days had grey stratus. How many days did not have stratus?
pool.hint: Take the stratus days away from all the days.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b} days without stratus.

pool.prompt: Why does a big storm cloud look dark underneath?
choices: It is so thick that little sunlight gets through
pool.hint: Think about light trying to pass through a very thick cloud.
pool.explain: The water in it is clean. The cloud is so thick that it blocks most of the sunlight, so its base looks dark.

pool.prompt: Which is true about water vapour?
choices: It is a gas you cannot see
It is the white part of a cloud
It is the same as smoke
pool.hint: Can you see the water vapour in the air around you right now?
pool.explain: Water vapour is an invisible gas. The white we see in a cloud is the tiny drops it turned into.
